title: Oil set for weekly surge on Mideast supply fears, Russian diesel deal uncertainty
full_text:
Nasdaq notches worst week since late June with a 4.5% slide as AI trade suffers
Investing.com -- Oil prices rose more than 3% on Friday and were on track for sharp weekly gains, boosted by Middle East supply disruption fears and uncertainty tied to a U.S. deal with Russia to supply diesel to the global markets.
At 15:31 ET (19:31 GMT), Brent crude futures expiring in December, the global benchmark, climbed 3.4% to $109.48 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures expiring in November advanced 3.3% to $101.17 a barrel. For the week, Brent was up 4.5% and WTI had gained 10.1%. Get more oil market insights by subscribing to InvestingPro
Attacks keep traders on edge
While overall Middle East crude flows have largely recovered to near pre-war levels, supply fears have been elevated amid a step up in Iranian attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and furious fighting between Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-backed government in Yemen. The conflict between the latter two has exacerbated worries over threats to oil flows in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Iran has increased its strikes on commercial ships transiting Hormuz in recent weeks as it remains at loggerheads with the U.S. over control of the waterway.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure and airports this week, resulting in 13 deaths at the King Khalid International Airport last weekend. The Houthis on Thursday targeted the Presidential Palace in Aden, the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Energy market participants also assessed a recent report that the U.S. was considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that transport oil and derivatives from sanctioned countries such as Russia, Iran, and Venezuela. The measure aims to bring down global freight rates and help cool runaway fuel prices, although whether it would proceed is unclear.
According to Kpler, the sanctions relief plan "may do little to alleviate record freight rates."
"Of approximately 160 OFAC-sanctioned (very large crude carriers), Kpler estimates that only 24 could potentially return to mainstream trade after accounting for vessel age and ownership restrictions," the shipping tracker said on Friday.
Diesel remains in the spotlight
Elsewhere, in an attempt to help bring down soaring prices of diesel, President Donald Trump has announced a major diesel supply deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Diesel supply disruptions were in focus after Ukraine said it would resume attacking Russia’s energy infrastructure, despite Trump’s attempts to forge an energy ceasefire between the two countries.
"Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump said in a Newsmax interview on Thursday. "If they’re going to end up with a settlement of some kind, they’re not going to do it with him. He doesn’t want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn’t," the U.S. president added. Last weekend Trump said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president.
"This ’Diesel Deal’ will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets. But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war," Zelenskyy said in an address at a European Council meeting on Friday.
The diesel agreement has also faced bipartisan backlash in Washington. A group of 18 U.S. Representatives comprised of 17 Democrats and 1 Republican introduced legislation on Friday to block the deal.
"Can Russia actually supply the diesel? Broadly speaking, yes. Given ongoing exports of nearly 150 KBD and the potential political value to Putin from this arrangement, we think these volumes can be managed or prioritized. Ultimately, we think Russia’s ability to meaningfully increase diesel exports will hinge on refining restarts and seasonal fluctuations in Russian demand," Walt Chancellor, energy strategist at Macquarie, said.
"Every bit helps, but we don’t expect this agreement to significantly change the underlying situation with Russian diesel," he added.
Separately, the International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to release over 20 million barrels of diesel, and signaled it will speed up the release of any oil remaining from an emergency reserve release pledged in March.
However, the IEA warned that global diesel markets could remain tight well into 2027. The group also projected a decline in global oil demand this year.

title: Jio’s $3.2 billion IPO tests investor appetite as Ambani legacy faces scrutiny
full_text:

Investing.com -- Reliance Industries’ (NSE) telecom unit Jio Platforms is preparing a $3.2 billion initial public offering, testing investor demand amid growing scrutiny of its valuation and growth prospects.
The offering, scheduled to open on October 21, is expected to become India’s largest IPO, marking a major milestone for billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s business empire.
Jio plans to sell shares at between 1,065 and 1,119 rupees each, valuing the company at approximately $108 billion at the upper end of the range.
That represents a discount to rival Bharti Airtel’s (NSE) market capitalisation of around $125 billion.
The valuation follows questions from institutional investors about Jio’s ability to justify a premium over its competitor and generate additional revenue from digital services beyond telecommunications.
Despite those concerns, the offering has attracted more than $20 billion in bids, with international investors including Fidelity Management & Research, Allianz and Capital Group expressing interest.
Akash Ambani, Jio’s 34-year-old managing director and Mukesh Ambani’s eldest son, is leading the listing.
The transaction comes nearly five decades after Reliance’s landmark 1977 IPO, which helped popularise direct equity ownership among Indian households.
However, India’s investor landscape has changed significantly.
The country now has more than 130 million registered stock market investors, with nearly 40% aged under 30, according to National Stock Exchange data.
Younger investors are increasingly focused on earnings growth, valuations and short-term returns rather than longstanding corporate reputations.
A 2024 study by India’s securities regulator found that retail investors sold 40% of their IPO allocations within a week of listing.
Reliance shares have declined 23% this year, putting the conglomerate on course for its worst annual performance since 2011.
Jio’s market debut will therefore test whether its telecommunications dominance and digital expansion strategy can attract investors seeking sustainable growth rather than relying on the Ambani family’s historical appeal.

title: Exclusive-US holds more secret talks with Myanmar’s military-backed rulers in Tokyo, sources say
full_text:
Nasdaq notches worst week since late June with a 4.5% slide as AI trade suffers
By Simon Lewis, Poppy McPherson and John Geddie
WASHINGTON/TOKYO, Oct 16 (Reuters) - The US and Myanmar’s military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup.
Earlier talks in Myanmar’s capital Naypyitaw in mid-September focused on securing the release of an American businessman and shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could pave the way for broader discussions, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters previously reported.
It was not immediately clear exactly what the two sides discussed at last week’s talks, disclosed to Reuters by three people with knowledge of the engagement. The people, including one US official, all spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the meeting.
US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance again led the Tokyo talks, which involved more than a dozen US officials, one of the people said. Reuters could not establish who represented Myanmar.
The US State Department declined to comment on Vance’s presence in the delegation but said the bureau he heads was not playing a leading role on US policy toward Myanmar.
The department’s Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs is "shaping, implementing and engaging on" US policy toward the country, a spokesperson said, while Vance’s Bureau of Intelligence and Research "informs policy makers but does not lead on policy."
"The United States does not comment on the content and parameters of purported sensitive discussions," the spokesperson said, adding that the engagement with Myanmar "is rooted in the desire to achieve practical wins for the American people — particularly those impacted by transnational crime."
A spokesperson for Myanmar’s military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment.
Asked about its role in hosting the talks, Japan’s Foreign Ministry said in an emailed statement it had been "communicating as necessary" with both sides but declined to comment on specific diplomatic exchanges.
Last month’s meeting in Naypyitaw between Vance and Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president, Min Aung Hlaing, provided an opening for broader discussions, people familiar with those talks previously told Reuters. The quick return to the negotiating table in Tokyo suggests both sides are keen to keep the dialogue going.
A major focus of the US push is securing Myanmar’s help in shutting down scam hubs that run romance and other frauds and have swindled Americans out of billions of dollars, the people said.
Researchers say many scam operations are based in areas controlled by army-backed militia, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar’s leaders are serious about enforcement. Myanmar’s military-backed government has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centres.
US officials have also discussed access to Myanmar’s large deposits of heavy rare earths, which are used in products ranging from electric vehicles to wind turbines. US officials acknowledge significant obstacles: the deposits are largely located in territory controlled by ethnic armed groups fighting the military, while China, the main buyer of Myanmar rare earths, could balk at any US role.
The US last week lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country’s military, saying the move was part of a new approach to the country.
"This approach highlights the importance of pursuing dialogue with all groups involved in Burma’s civil war and commits to re-examining the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country," the State Department said of the sanctions move.
Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including for his role in the coup and crushing a subsequent popular uprising, and the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington declared a genocide. The armed forces have killed thousands of people in airstrikes since the putsch, which sparked widespread civil war, the United Nations says.
The latest engagements in Japan show the Trump administration views Myanmar through a "purely transactionalist lens," said Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank.
"The critical minerals and rare earths that Myanmar holds are viewed as probably the chief strategic asset that Washington is interested in within Myanmar," Marston said.
JAPAN’S ROLE UNCLEAR
It is unclear whether Japan has any stake in the US-Myanmar talks beyond playing host, including for earlier talks in the Japanese capital in June, but there are signs that Tokyo is also moving to re-engage with Myanmar.
Japan’s acting envoy to Myanmar met with the foreign minister of Myanmar’s military-backed government earlier this month in their first known public engagement. Tokyo does not formally recognise the administration.
That meeting followed a September visit by Japanese ruling party lawmaker Hiromichi Watanabe to Naypyitaw, which he said was aimed at restarting bilateral cooperation and resuming development aid to Myanmar, according to the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper.
Japan’s Foreign Ministry said the acting envoy raised issues such as protection for Japanese nationals and support for Japanese companies, while Watanabe’s trip was in his capacity as an individual member of parliament and "does not in any way prejudge" the position of the government.
Watanabe told Reuters his trip was aimed at preparing the environment to normalise relations, though he acknowledged that barriers remained.
Japan condemned the military’s 2021 overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government but stopped short of joining the US and other Western governments in imposing sanctions on junta leaders and military-linked entities.
Tokyo was one of Myanmar’s largest foreign investors, seeking to counter China’s influence in one of Asia’s last frontier markets. Unlike numerous Western firms, many Japanese companies remained despite the turmoil that followed the 2021 coup.
Around 300 Japanese companies still operate in Myanmar, down from more than 400 in 2020, according to Japan’s trade promotion agency, JETRO.

title: Trump waives key Russia-related sanctions, tariffs before they take effect under new law
full_text:
Nasdaq notches worst week since late June with a 4.5% slide as AI trade suffers
By Kanishka Singh and Jasper Ward
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs days before they were to take effect under a law he signed last month, including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas.
In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Russia and publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Weeks before the US midterm elections in which Trump’s Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked raising oil prices even further while Americans already face increased costs largely attributed to the US-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said.
The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
The order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that "further action is appropriate."
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in the order.
Countries such as China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, have raised concerns about the Russia sanctions bill.
Beijing has said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.
The law allows the president to waive sanctions simply by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest.
US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, blasted Trump for the waiver, saying he was giving in to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement.
Trump had also faced criticism from several US senators, including some Republicans, over a recent diesel deal with Russia in which Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian exports and Russia agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. The lawmakers who criticized the deal said it would help fund Russia’s war efforts.

title: Trump threatens California officials with imprisonment over stance on mail ballots
full_text:
Nasdaq notches worst week since late June with a 4.5% slide as AI trade suffers
By Jasper Ward
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department on Friday warned Los Angeles County and California election officials they could be liable as abettors of a federal crime if they count mail ballots returned by more than 20,000 people the Trump administration says are probably noncitizens.
The warning to the Los Angeles County Assistant Counsel Peter Bollinger came less than three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections and days after the department gave California 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action. On Thursday, the Justice Department sued California to block the state from counting the ballots.
"Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, wrote in a letter released on Friday. McCotter called on the county and California’s secretary of state to reconsider their refusal to take steps that the Trump administration argues are needed to deter voter fraud.
US President Donald Trump shared the letter on Truth Social with the comment: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan were copied on McCotter’s letter.
The county’s counsel office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Weber’s office referred Reuters to an earlier statement in which she said the Justice Department’s attempts to "unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."
An earlier letter that McCotter sent on Tuesday to Weber and Logan said the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" that were sent mail-in ballots from California.
Los Angeles County Counsel Dawyn R. Harrison said on Thursday the county cannot comply with the Justice Department’s requests because the Trump administration did not explain how the list was made. Friday’s letter from McCotter said the Justice Department used "internal immigration records" and data matching.
In July, Trump said his administration had uncovered evidence of more than 275,000 non-citizens registered to vote, but it was not clear how many had actually voted.
In some previous cases, systems intended to verify citizenship have mistakenly flagged some naturalized US citizens as noncitizens. Studies have found that noncitizens casting actual ballots is exceedingly uncommon.
Since July, the Justice Department has ramped up prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. The White House has also pushed federal agencies to accelerate their review of at least 47 state voter rolls obtained by the Department of Homeland Security, according to an internal email seen by Reuters.

Under this scenario, using advanced AI would resemble assembling the world’s leading experts to solve a business problem, with systems capable of identifying tasks independently rather than simply following instructions.
The technology could eventually become widely accessible, with capabilities comparable to today’s most advanced AI models running directly on smartphones, tablets and laptops.

Companies adopting superintelligence could gain substantial competitive advantages, potentially forcing rivals to integrate similar technology or risk losing market share.
However, the analysts cautioned that technological capability alone would not guarantee widespread adoption.
Physical infrastructure, regulatory requirements and organisational resistance could delay implementation, particularly in heavily regulated industries.
Electricity, land, equipment and operating licences could become increasingly valuable as sophisticated cognitive capabilities become cheaper.
The report also identified significant obstacles to achieving superintelligence, including computing requirements, financing constraints and the difficulty of developing AI systems that reliably improve themselves.
Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle are expected to spend nearly $800 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, potentially exceeding $1 trillion annually through 2030.

Even without reaching that milestone, AI adoption could deliver substantial productivity improvements and economic benefits as businesses integrate increasingly capable systems into everyday operations.

Investing.com -- Anthropic is offering Blackstone (NYSE) a double-digit return on debt financing for a $60 billion AI chip deal, the Financial Times first reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The financing package, known as Project North Star, would support Anthropic’s acquisition of approximately 1.5 gigawatts of Google’s custom tensor processing units (TPUs).

The remaining $9 billion in junior debt is expected to be offered to other investors in the coming months, potentially at lower yields.
Anthropic previously raised approximately $4.4 billion through a similar financing arrangement, Project Big Sky, at an 8.5% interest rate four months ago.
The higher borrowing costs reflect growing investor demands for compensation as AI developers seek substantial funding for computing infrastructure.
The latest package also includes about $42 billion in senior debt guaranteed by Broadcom (NASDAQ), which collaborates with Google to develop the chips.
Anthropic received a credit rating one notch below investment grade from KBRA in June, with the new junior debt expected to receive a similar assessment.
The company is seeking investment-grade status, which could substantially reduce future borrowing costs.
The debt could become tradable in the institutional 144A bond market once the financing is drawn down in 2027.

title: IMF members call for more support amid war shocks, ’advanced intelligence’ risks
full_text:
Nasdaq notches worst week since late June with a 4.5% slide as AI trade suffers
By David Lawder
BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - International Monetary Fund member countries called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by negative spillovers from wars and high energy prices, and said economic risks remain tilted to the downside.
And while there has been a boost to investment and trade from "advanced intelligence technologies", they also carried risks, the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee said in a statement after a meeting in Bangkok.
"Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security," said the statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chair of the IMFC.
The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender.
Al-Jadaan told Reuters that the language of the statement was agreed by all members.
Earlier this week, the United States was pressing fellow IMF members to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" in the statement, in line with US President Donald Trump’s preferred name for the technology, a senior US Treasury official told Reuters.
The final version of the chair’s statement contained no reference to artificial intelligence.
It said the uncertain impact of "advanced intelligence technologies", along with rising bond yields in major economies that spill over to highly indebted economies, "could amplify macro-financial vulnerabilities."
"Rapid technological change, demographic shifts, more frequent extreme weather events and natural disasters, and geoeconomic fragmentation are compounding policy tradeoffs," the statement said.
The member economies agreed to support countries that undertake reforms and address debt vulnerabilities, with specific attention to low-income and vulnerable middle-income countries and conflict-affected states.
"We encourage increasing support to countries with sustainable debt and strong reform and growth enhancing agenda, but facing short-term financing challenges," the statement said, noting that several members had provided assurances of support to the IMF’s Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which supports poor and developing countries.

WASHINGTON, Oct 17 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is blaming senior aides and political operatives for a faltering midterm strategy, questioning campaign spending, faulting redistricting and second-guessing candidate choices as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, said three people familiar with internal discussions.
Trump is not on the November 3 ballot but repeatedly tells supporters to pretend that he is, hoping to mobilize voters who might otherwise skip the election. He has embarked on a frenetic campaign schedule while largely avoiding acknowledging his own role in shaping the strategy and how his unpopularity is weighing on Republican candidates in competitive races.
Much of the friction has centered on James Blair, the longtime aide who runs Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc., and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who until now had largely escaped criticism. Trump has faulted Blair’s handling of campaign funds, while some White House officials and allies have questioned Wiles’ oversight of the political operation.
As Trump questions why campaign spending has failed to improve Republican polling numbers, his advisers are also blaming one another. Wiles has pointed to Blair, while Blair has faulted the White House legislative affairs team, one of the people said.
"What’s really happening is a circular firing squad," the person said.
Opinion polls suggest Democrats will win the House of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call. Losing the House would hamper Trump’s legislative agenda in the final two years of his term and give Democrats subpoena power to investigate his administration.
Trump defended Wiles on Friday, calling her "smart" and "tough" and saying she would remain in her job. "Susie is here, and she’s going to be here for a long time," he said.
White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the sources’ characterization, saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Wiles did not respond to a request for comment.
TRUMP HAS LONG DISTANCED HIMSELF FROM POLITICAL SETBACKS
Trump has long sought to distance himself from political setbacks. He refused to accept his defeat in the 2020 election and said ahead of the 2022 midterm results that he deserved "all the credit" if Republicans won but "should not be blamed at all" if they lost. More recently, he has reminded audiences that the president’s party typically struggles in midterm elections.
But Trump helped devise and drive some of the strategies he is now questioning, including the redistricting effort and candidate choices shaped by his personal loyalties or grievances. His approval rating is at the lowest point of his presidency, weighed down by voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the Iran war.
Trump’s frustrations with his political team spilled into public view after Blair and Chris LaCivita, who co-managed Trump’s 2024 campaign, traveled in early October to Republika Srpska, a self-governing region of Bosnia. The New York Times reported the men received substantial payments to advise the regional government ahead of local elections.
Trump distanced himself from both men, describing them as "outside consultants" in an October 7 Truth Social post and warning that if he found a conflict of interest, he would "terminate them, immediately!"
Senior White House officials questioned why Blair was taking on lucrative work overseas when he was supposed to be overseeing the final stretch of the Republican campaign, three people said.
One person said Wiles approved the trip without informing Trump, raising questions about how closely she was overseeing his political advisers.
For Trump, the larger concern is that Blair’s outside work has distracted him from his political responsibilities, two people said.
In a statement, Blair said: "All of this mudslinging is ridiculous, and counterproductive. President Trump and me are focused on helping Republicans win in November. Every other Republican should be doing the same."
In a separate statement, LaCivita said: "President Trump and his team are and always have been focused on the midterms. That’s demonstrated through the money, message and motivation that the president is bringing on the road and all year. Texas is a particular concern. Republicans redrew the state’s congressional map to gain seats, but the strategy relies in part on Hispanic voters turning out as they did for the 2024 election. Opinion polls suggest that support may be difficult to replicate amid concerns about the cost of living and Trump’s handling of the economy. Some Republicans fear the new boundaries could backfire, leaving incumbents more vulnerable instead of giving the party an advantage.
"The redistricting diced up the Trump voters too much," one of the sources said.
Trump had said Blair was expected to return to the White House after the midterms, describing his departure as a "short leave of absence." But two sources said his return was now unlikely. "He’s not coming back. That is not happening," one of them said.

Trump "may be annoyed at certain things but she has effectively kept that machine going," a fourth source close to the White House said.

title: Explainer-Could hackers get inside my fridge?
full_text:
Nasdaq notches worst week since late June with a 4.5% slide as AI trade suffers
By Hugo Lhomedet and Leo Marchandon
Oct 13 (Reuters) - Hackers who sabotaged refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets exploited the growing connectivity of equipment that was once largely mechanical.
From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.
CAN HACKERS REALLY GET INTO MY FRIDGE?
In theory, yes. If a device is connected to the internet, directly or through an app, cloud service or home network, it can potentially be hacked.
In 2015, researchers demonstrated at a Las Vegas hacking conference how a Samsung smart refrigerator could be compromised, allowing them to intercept some of the internet traffic passing through the device.
In many cases, attackers are more interested in stealing data, disrupting services or using connected devices as a way into a larger network.
WHAT HOUSEHOLD DEVICES COULD BE HACKED?
The most common targets are devices connected to the internet and controlled remotely.
These include security cameras, video doorbells, alarm systems, smart locks, thermostats and central heating systems. Smart appliances such as refrigerators, ovens and washing machines can also be vulnerable if they are connected to the wider internet. Even some toothbrushes are now internet-connected.
Routers, not appliances, account for more than three-quarters of all attacks on connected devices, according to security-industry data.
The number of such devices has grown rapidly as manufacturers have added internet connectivity to products that were once entirely mechanical.
WHAT COULD A HACKER ACTUALLY DO?
Once inside a device, a hacker can generally do one of two things: gather information or take control of the device.
A camera can show the inside of a home, a device with a microphone can pick up sound, and a compromised router can expose everything that travels through the network.
Hackers who take control of a device can switch it on or off, change settings or lock users out of their accounts. A compromised thermostat could affect heating, while a hacked freezer or refrigerator could disrupt temperature controls.
In more serious cases, attackers may use poorly secured devices to gain access to other systems on the same network or to steal personal information linked to online accounts.
COULD HACKERS TAKE OVER MY CAR, ELECTRICITY OR WATER SUPPLY?
Cybersecurity researchers have repeatedly demonstrated vulnerabilities in connected vehicles.
In 2015, researchers remotely took control of a moving Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, forcing the recall of about 1.4 million vehicles and the deployment of software fixes.
Nearly a decade later, researchers disclosed a flaw that allowed them to track, unlock and start certain Kia vehicles using only a licence plate number. The researchers said they reported the vulnerabilities to Kia, which fixed them within months, and there was no evidence they had been exploited in real-world attacks.
Modern vehicles and aircraft are also designed with extensive safety and backup systems.
Critical infrastructure such as power and water networks generally has multiple layers of security, monitoring and regulation that are not present in consumer devices.
That does not mean they are immune from cyber attacks, but they are typically much harder targets than a household appliance connected to a home Wi‑Fi network.
HOW CAN PEOPLE PROTECT THEIR DEVICES?
Cybersecurity experts generally recommend changing default passwords, enabling two-factor authentication where available and regularly installing software updates.
Consumers should also remove or replace devices that no longer receive security updates, keep most devices on a local network and only connect products to the wider internet when there is a clear reason to do so.
The simplest rule is often the most effective: the fewer connected devices you have, the fewer potential entry points exist for attackers.

BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - High debt levels, rising debt-service costs and a sharp drop in official development assistance are forcing developing countries and institutions that help them to rethink development and look for new sources of funding, including from the private sector.
World Bank President Ajay Banga, who has led a drive that has more than tripled the private capital flowing to development projects since 2022, told the annual IMF and World Bank meetings that changes were needed to help countries address headwinds posed by persistent conflicts, a drop in official development assistance and rising debt burdens.
A huge demographic challenge was also unfolding, he said, with some 1.2 billion young people likely to join the job market in the next 10 to 15 years, but only 400 million jobs in sight.
The answer, Banga said, would depend on bringing public finance, private investment, philanthropy and technology together to meet each country’s needs.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he would make debt restructuring and other help for the poorest countries a key theme for Britain’s upcoming G20 presidency.
But he said the private sector needed to step up since Britain and other rich nations could not provide the same level of support as during the last big debt forgiveness push at the turn of the millennium.
"The risks of lending to emerging markets have been overestimated and the risk of default has been overestimated," he told a panel on Wednesday hosted by the Rockefeller Foundation, a private US foundation that works on development.
Developing countries are also looking for answers outside the two Bretton Woods institutions, disappointed by the response to high debt levels, climate change, worsening inequality and geopolitical challenges.
"The world has, in many ways, changed for the worse since 2023," Shekhar Aiyar, director and chief executive of the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations, told an event hosted by the Center for Global Development this week.
"Developing countries have been caught in a downward spiral of decelerating growth and increased vulnerability ... at the same time, there has been a vast scaling back of bilateral aid."
International aid from OECD Development Assistance Committee donor countries fell 23% in real terms in 2025, marking the biggest annual drop in the history of ODA. The top five donors — the US, Germany, UK, Japan and France — all cut aid, together accounting for 96% of the total drop.
Meanwhile, according to UNCTAD — the official UN body responsible for trade, investment and development issues — developing countries’ combined external debt stock reached $12.3 trillion in the same year, up by half a trillion from 2024.
NEW PARTNERSHIPS AND APPROACHES
US President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs have added to strains and prompted many developing countries and emerging markets to forge new trade partnerships that do not include the United States.
Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman told an Atlantic Council broadcast that countries like hers were plowing ahead with more bilateral partnerships.
"I feel this approach of ’Yes, we want multilateralism, but yet we’re not waiting for it, we are going ahead with bilateral,’ has really rewarded India," Sitharaman said.
Eric LeCompte, executive director of Jubilee USA Network, which advocates for debt relief, said this year’s meetings were a big disappointment for developing countries, providing no new initiative to help those already facing steep debt-service payments and now saddled with soaring borrowing costs.
He said the IMF failed to reach critical mass to launch its expanded Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which lends to low-income countries at low interest rates, and barely mentioned its Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust, which provides grants for debt relief to the world’s poorest countries.
"There was a lot of information about how challenging problems are, but we saw hardly any action," he said, aside from tweaks to debt restructuring plans by the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable. "We were expecting more," he said.
Jean Saldanha, director of the European Network on Debt and Development, asked: "Where are the emergency measures to stop countries in the Global South being forced to spend more on debt than on health and education? And where are the serious policy responses to the escalating climate emergency, boosted by a Super El Niño?"
"The least-developed countries have said loud and clear they need more climate grants, less debt, simpler access and faster disbursements," she said.
Muhammad Al Jasser, who chairs the Islamic Development Bank group, told Reuters there was growing interest in securing private sector funds to augment increasingly scarce public resources.
"The challenges are huge. We’re not going to solve them either single-handedly or even collectively in a short period of time, but I think we are (heading) in the right direction," he said, adding his bank was aiming to deploy $10 billion in financing next year.

Corruption, a lack of jobs and a general feeling that the government does not work for them have created a deep-seated anger that spilled over this week, when young protesters swarmed the capital Tirana, setting fire to government buildings and banks and hurling pavement stones at police.
The government and the police have condemned the violence. According to police figures, 500 protestors have been detained, 330 of whom have been released. Some 120 police and 45 protesters have been injured, the figures show, although the protester figure is likely higher given that many injuries have gone unrecorded.
Albania’s unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe, including in France, where high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities.
YOUTH PROTESTS THREATEN RAMA’S RULE
"The country is amazing, but ... the wrong policies that have been implemented by this political elite are completely against what the Albanian communities and Albanian citizens have been asking and seeking for so long," Koceku said during the protests on Friday as police fired tear gas and water cannon at protesters nearby.
Rama, a former basketball player, has been in power since 2013, half Koceku’s life. He won a fourth term in elections last year but his administration has since been dogged by corruption scandals.
Rama denies wrongdoing and this week told Reuters that he would not step down.
"Governments are changed through democratic elections and we had them last year, not through violence," he said.
Still, the protests represent the biggest threat to his rule yet.
They follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by plans to build a luxury resort on Albania’s pristine southern coastline. The project, whose backers include US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, has faced legal challenges.
Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was wrongfully sold for the development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied.
Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers’ dispute. He did not respond to requests for comment.
That was not the only controversy for Rama’s government. Last year, prosecutors alleged that his deputy prime minister was involved in doling out construction contracts to favoured companies, charges Rama and the deputy deny.
"I didn’t agree, especially with the policies that they were implementing against nature, and our land and our Albania," Koceku said.
This week, protesters said they had resorted to violence because they had not felt heard.
The Kushner-backed project upset Koceku, who has a close relationship with the land. She is from the remote mountains of northern Albania where her family runs a small, no-frills guest house on the shore of a lake.
"Our country is the Albanian people," she said, the air around her thick with acrid tear gas. "They create the future, they create the now, and they are the ones who can bring our country forward. Not a single person, not a single government."

He has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness.

Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s secretary of state, said on Friday that Leo may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward "according to the condition of his health". It is unusual for a cardinal to say openly that a pope might need to modify his routine.

Investing.com -- Another downgrade of France’s sovereign credit rating is unlikely to threaten the European Union’s creditworthiness, according to a UBS research report examining the bloc’s financial safeguards.
In an October 16 report, UBS analysts said France’s deteriorating credit profile would not automatically trigger an EU downgrade, given the diversification of member-state support and differences in rating agency methodologies.
The assessment comes ahead of Moody’s scheduled review of France on October 23.
Moody’s currently rates France Aa3 with a negative outlook, while S&P and Fitch assign A+ ratings with stable outlooks.
The EU itself maintains an Aaa rating from Moody’s, AAA from Fitch and AA+ from S&P, all with stable outlooks.
The analysts estimated that France would need to fall to Baa3 under Moody’s methodology or BBB under S&P’s before its deterioration alone affected their respective weighted-average assessments of member-state credit quality.
Fitch’s methodology presents even less direct exposure because France is excluded from the agency’s pool of AAA-rated countries supporting the EU’s creditworthiness.
Instead, the analysts identified Germany as a more significant potential vulnerability, particularly if weakening sovereign ratings reduced highly rated members’ capacity to cover EU debt obligations.
They also highlighted safeguards allowing the European Commission to request additional contributions from other members if a country fails to meet its obligations.
However, these arrangements have never been tested.
Beyond sovereign ratings, political resistance to further European fiscal integration represents a longer-term concern.
The analysts pointed to proposals in France to reduce EU budget contributions and growing opposition in Germany to additional joint borrowing.
Nevertheless, existing budget commitments provide some protection against abrupt funding changes.
The analysts concluded that political resistance could ultimately constrain the expansion and permanence of the EU bond market without necessarily undermining the creditworthiness of outstanding debt.
